content.text: {"relation": "DIVERGENT", "consensus_summary": "Mainstream consensus treats the new moon as the calendrical observance beginning the lunar month (understood astronomically as the dark conjunction or first visible crescent), whose Christian symbolic significance is defined by Colossians 2:16-17: a ceremonial 'shadow' fulfilled in Christ, with secondary associations of renewal/new beginnings, prophetic critique of empty ritual, and eschatological perpetual worship (Isa 66:23; Ezek 46).", "book_summary": "The book redefines the 'new moon' (renewed moon) as the FULL moon — the phase that marks the start of the month — associated with the opened east gate of Ezekiel 46 and functioning as the sign of the appointed times. It explicitly rejects the commonly taught identification of the new moon as the dark conjunction or first visible crescent.", "consensus_core_identification": "The new moon = the monthly observance at the start of the lunar month (dark/crescent phase), symbolically a ceremonial shadow fulfilled in Christ, with renewal and appointed-time connotations.", "book_core_identification": "The new moon = the full moon, the phase that begins the month, the sign of the appointed times seen in the opened east gate.", "core_relation": "CONTRADICTS", "extension_relation": "DIFFERENT_REFERENT", "boundary_disagreement": "The disagreement is not about symbolic scope but about the physical identity of the referent itself: the book locates the month-beginning 'new moon' at the full-moon phase, whereas every consensus response presupposes the standard dark-conjunction/first-crescent identification. The set of actual days denoted by 'new moon' would differ by roughly half a lunar cycle.", "material_contradiction": "The book states the new moon is the full moon; the consensus (and the book's own common-view note) holds it is the dark conjunction or first visible crescent. A given lunar phase cannot be both the full moon and the dark/crescent moon, so accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus identification of the referent. No consensus response or listed alternative (including the rare lunar-sabbath calendrical reconstructions) identifies the new moon as the full moon.", "rationale": "Both readings agree the new moon marks the start of the month and functions as a sign of appointed times, so there is a shared category (calendrical appointed time). But the book's central and distinctive claim replaces the standard astronomical identification of that referent with the full moon, explicitly against the commonly taught view. This is not a boundary refinement of the consensus's symbolic reading (shadow fulfilled in Christ / renewal); it is a replacement of what the term physically denotes. Hence DIVERGENT with a contradicted core and a different referent extensionally, even though the same scriptural occasions are in view.", "citation_support": "INSUFFICIENT", "strongest_objection": "One could argue the book merely refines the same referent — the biblical month-opening observance attested in the very same texts (Ps 81:3; 1 Sam 20; Ezek 46) — and only recalibrates which lunar phase it falls on, which might suggest REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. Additionally, Psalm 81:3's Hebrew 'keseh' is sometimes rendered 'full moon,' which a defender could claim gives the entry more textual footing than the KJV excerpts show. However, the book's own common-view note frames its claim as a direct denial of the standard identification, and the printed KJV citations nowhere state the new moon is the full moon, so the contradiction stands on the given materials.", "confidence": "high"}
